A California-based Apple user has filed a proposed class action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading consumers over the privacy protections of its "Hide My Email" feature. Here are the details.

Apple Sued Over Alleged 'Hide My Email' Vulnerability

404 Media recently reported that Apple had been aware of a vulnerability allegedly capable of exposing the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias for over a year.

Apple's "Hide My Email" feature allows users to create unique, randomly generated email addresses that forward messages to their personal inbox, so they do not have to provide their real email address when signing up for apps, websites, or newsletters.

The feature is offered for free through "Sign in with Apple," while an expanded version, included with iCloud+ plans (starting at $0.99 per month), lets users create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher warned Apple in June 2025 about a vulnerability that could expose the real email address behind a "Hide My Email" alias.

Apple reportedly acknowledged the report about a month later, but allegedly failed to address the issue. In March 2026, the company claimed it had fixed the vulnerability, but the researcher found it was still exploitable.

The following is an excerpt from 404 Media:

Regarding the lawsuit (reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez stated:

Apple has been aware of this issue for over a year, and the vulnerability remains unfixed—yet Apple continues to profit from "Hide My Email" and its promises of privacy. The plaintiff is one of millions of customers who pay Apple for iCloud+ and rely on Apple's claim that "Hide My Email" will keep their personal email address from being disclosed. Both the plaintiff and the class members pay Apple for privacy protection—iCloud+ users through the premium portion of the iCloud+ subscription fee, and all Apple customers through the premium portion of Apple product prices, as Apple markets its products as including enhanced privacy protections and features such as "Hide My Email."

The lawsuit also claims this is not an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple's randomized MAC address feature could expose users' real hardware identifiers.

The complaint also states that the total claims of the proposed class members exceed $5 million (excluding interest and legal fees), though it does not explain how that figure was calculated.

Alvarez filed on behalf of himself and other allegedly affected Apple customers, asking the court to certify the case as a class action covering the following four proposed user groups:

  • All Apple customers nationwide who have purchased a device and used "Hide My Email";
  • A California subset of the above users;
  • All iCloud+ subscribers nationwide who have used the feature;
  • A California subset of iCloud+ subscribers.

He is seeking a jury trial and, in addition to unspecified monetary damages, is asking the court to order Apple to fix the "Hide My Email" feature or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.

Do you think this class action should be certified? Let us know in the comments.
